claims.text: Functional decline is often recognized only after falls, gait impairment, or reduced mobility become visible.
claims.poster_quote: Functional decline is often recognized only after falls, gait impairment, or reduced mobility become visible.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Functional decline - encompassing gait impairment, reduced mobility, and fall risk - affects more than one-third of adults over 65 and contributes to approximately three million emergency visits and $50 billion in annual U.S. healthcare expenditures. Despite this burden, functional decline lacks an automated early warning system embedded in routine clinical workflows. It is typically recognized only after observable impairment or a fall event, when the pre-clinical prevention window has closed.
claims.reason: The claim is directly supported by the provided evidence in the introduction section of the paper, which states that functional decline is typically recognized only after observable impairment or a fall event.

claims.text: Routine biomarkers may deteriorate earlier without triggering alerts.
claims.poster_quote: Routine biomarkers may deteriorate earlier without triggering alerts.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Functional decline in older adults is typically recognized only after falls or observable gait impairment, closing the window for prevention. We investigated whether temporal trajectories of routine biomarkers — already recorded but rarely analyzed longitudinally — can identify patients in the pre-clinical phase of mobility decline.
claims.reason: The abstract explicitly states that routine biomarkers are already recorded but rarely analyzed longitudinally, suggesting they may deteriorate earlier without triggering alerts.

claims.text: Existing tools capture one timepoint, while biomarker trajectories may reveal an earlier prevention window.
claims.poster_quote: Existing tools capture one timepoint, while biomarker trajectories may reveal an earlier prevention window.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Existing frailty tools, such as the Fried phenotype, the Short Physical Performance Battery, and the Timed Up-and-Go, require structured functional assessments, manual scoring, or dedicated patient interaction not consistently embedded in primary care workflows. Even when administered, they capture a single timepoint rather than the trajectory of physiologic change.
claims.reason: The introduction section explicitly states that existing tools capture a single timepoint, while biomarker trajectories may reveal more predictive information.

claims.text: Robustness analyses separated physiology from demographics, utilization, and observation patterns.
claims.poster_quote: Robustness analyses separated physiology from demographics, utilization, and observation patterns.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Our contributions are: (1) a pseudo-index cohort design preventing immortal time bias; (2) trajectory features including slope, variability, and directional change for twelve routine biomarkers; (3) a four-algorithm comparative evaluation using out-of-fold predictions with DeLong significance testing; (4) a 1:1 age- and sex-matched sensitivity analysis isolating independent trajectory signal from demographic confounding; (5) a count-feature removal analysis disentangling physiologic signal from healthcare utilization artifacts - an instance of 'informative missingness' where measurement frequency itself correlates with disease severity.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly mentions robustness analyses that separate physiology from demographics, utilization, and observation patterns in the contributions section.

claims.text: The model is a passive digital biomarker using routine measurements, with no new tests, interaction, scoring, or functional assessment.
claims.poster_quote: The model is a passive digital biomarker using routine measurements, with no new tests, interaction, scoring, or functional assessment.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: This constraint is a deliberate design choice: it produces a model that functions as a passive digital biomarker, requiring no new data collection, patient interaction, or clinical workflow modification.
claims.reason: The discussion section explicitly states that the model functions as a passive digital biomarker, requiring no new tests, interaction, scoring, or functional assessment.

claims.text: Risk can update with each result, prompting physical therapy, fall screening, or geriatric assessment.
claims.poster_quote: Risk can update with each result, prompting physical therapy, fall screening, or geriatric assessment.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The model requires no new tests, no patient interaction, and no additional documentation. It runs as a background process, updating risk scores each time a new laboratory result is filed. At a clinical visit, the physician sees a single alert - 'Elevated functional decline risk - consider physical therapy referral or geriatric assessment' - while the pre-clinical intervention window remains open.
claims.reason: The discussion section explicitly states that risk can update with each result and suggests actions such as physical therapy, fall screening, or geriatric assessment.

claims.text: Isotonic calibration improved Brier score from 0.174 to 0.083 while preserving AUC.
claims.poster_quote: Isotonic calibration improved Brier score from 0.174 to 0.083 while preserving AUC.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Isotonic calibration reduced Brier score from 0.174 to 0.083 (52.3% improvement) without degrading discrimination (AUROC 0.797 vs. 0.796; Figure 4).
claims.reason: The results section explicitly states that isotonic calibration improved the Brier score from 0.174 to 0.083 while preserving AUC.

claims.text: Feature engineering fits existing EHR infrastructure and may support lower-contact, resource-constrained settings.
claims.poster_quote: Feature engineering fits existing EHR infrastructure and may support lower-contact, resource-constrained settings.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Our feature-engineered approach offers a pragmatic middle ground: it captures the key temporal dynamics (slope, variability, directional change) that distinguish declining patients while remaining compatible with standard tabular classifiers deployable in any EHR environment.
claims.reason: The discussion section explicitly states that feature engineering fits existing EHR infrastructure and supports deployment in resource-constrained settings.

claims.text: Routine biomarker trajectories identify mobility decline before clinical recognition, without medications, comorbidities, falls, assessments, or free text.
claims.poster_quote: We tested whether routine biomarker trajectories identify mobility decline before clinical recognition, without medications, comorbidities, falls, assessments, or free text.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Our model achieves AUROC 0.797 using only twelve laboratory biomarkers - no diagnosis codes, medications, functional assessments, or free-text processing.
claims.reason: The discussion section explicitly states that routine biomarker trajectories identify mobility decline without relying on medications, comorbidities, falls, assessments, or free text.

claims.text: Pseudo-index assignment prevented immortal time bias.
claims.poster_quote: Pseudo-index assignment prevented immortal time bias.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: A pseudo-index date was assigned by sampling uniformly at random within each control’s laboratory observation window (first to last measurement). This design preserves natural measurement history while preventing immortal time bias, a recognized source of inflated effect estimates in observational studies where controls are implicitly guaranteed survival to a fixed endpoint.
claims.reason: The methods section explicitly states that pseudo-index assignment was used to prevent immortal time bias.

claims.text: Prediction-horizon testing excluded recent pre-index measurements to assess earlier detection.
claims.poster_quote: Prediction-horizon testing excluded recent pre-index measurements to assess earlier detection.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: To evaluate the temporal lead time available for early detection, we assessed model discrimination when laboratory measurements within 3, 6, 9, and 12 months of the index date were excluded. This design simulates prospective screening where predictions must be made before clinical recognition of mobility decline.
claims.reason: The results section explicitly describes prediction-horizon testing that excluded recent pre-index measurements to assess earlier detection.

claims.text: Age and sex matching yielded AUROC 0.727 versus 0.680 for demographics alone.
claims.poster_quote: Age and sex matching yielded AUROC 0.727 versus 0.680 for demographics alone.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The matched trajectory model achieved AUROC 0.727 (0.723–0.731). This result enables a three-way signal decomposition: of the total 0.797 AUROC, 0.180 units above chance (0.5) are attributable to demographics (0.680 − 0.5), 0.047 to independent laboratory trajectory signal (0.727 − 0.680).
claims.reason: The results section explicitly states that age and sex matching yielded AUROC 0.727 versus 0.680 for demographics alone.

claims.text: Removing counts reduced AUROC from 0.797 to 0.789, preserving approximately 99% of discrimination.
claims.poster_quote: Removing counts reduced AUROC from 0.797 to 0.789, preserving approximately 99% of discrimination.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Removing count features yielded AUROC 0.789 (0.786–0.791), a reduction of 0.009 (DeLong p < 0.001).
claims.reason: The results section explicitly states that removing counts reduced AUROC from 0.797 to 0.789, preserving approximately 99% of discrimination.

claims.text: Cases had lower missingness throughout; albumin was 32.1% vs 51.4%, and hemoglobin 21.3% vs 37.0%.
claims.poster_quote: Cases had lower missingness throughout; albumin was 32.1% vs 51.4%, and hemoglobin 21.3% vs 37.0%.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Cases showed systematically lower missingness than controls across all biomarkers (Figure 1), with the largest differential for albumin (32.1% vs. 51.4%) and hemoglobin (21.3% vs. 37.0%).
claims.reason: The results section explicitly states that cases had lower missingness throughout, with specific percentages for albumin and hemoglobin.

claims.text: Twelve prespecified biomarkers were modeled over a three-year window, with all post-index measurements excluded.
claims.poster_quote: Twelve prespecified biomarkers were modeled over a three-year window, with all post-index measurements excluded.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Twelve biomarkers with established pathophysiologic links to functional decline were selected a priori... All measurements on or after the index date were excluded to prevent data leakage. The primary analysis used a three-year pre-index window (N = 297,861; 33,088 cases, 11.1%).
claims.reason: The methods section explicitly states that twelve biomarkers were modeled over a three-year window, with all post-index measurements excluded.

claims.text: Baseline used biomarker means; trajectories captured variability, first-to-last change, measurement count, and daily slope.
claims.poster_quote: Baseline used biomarker means; trajectories captured variability, first-to-last change, measurement count, and daily slope.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Baseline features used each biomarker’s mean value within the window. Trajectory features captured five per-biomarker descriptors: mean, standard deviation (intra-individual variability), delta (last minus first, directional change), count (measurement frequency), and linear slope (rate of change per day).
claims.reason: The methods section explicitly describes baseline using biomarker means and trajectories capturing variability, first-to-last change, measurement count, and daily slope.

claims.text: Penalized logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM were compared by five-fold cross-validation in N = 297,861.
claims.poster_quote: Penalized logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM were compared by five-fold cross-validation in N = 297,861.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Four algorithms were evaluated: (1) ℓ2-penalized logistic regression... (2) random forest... (3) XGBoost... and (4) LightGBM... All models were trained with 5-fold stratified cross-validation; out-of-fold (OOF) predictions across all folds were aggregated for unbiased evaluation.
claims.reason: The methods section explicitly states that penalized logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM were compared by five-fold cross-validation in N = 297,861.

claims.text: Missing values used training-fold medians; evaluation covered out-of-fold discrimination, calibration, and reclassification.
claims.poster_quote: Missing values used training-fold medians; evaluation covered out-of-fold discrimination, calibration, and reclassification.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Missing values were imputed with the median of each biomarker computed from the training partition of each cross-validation fold, ensuring held-out data never informed the imputed values and preventing data leakage. Primary discrimination was assessed by AUROC on OOF predictions with bootstrap 95% CIs (2,000 resampling iterations).
claims.reason: The methods section explicitly states that missing values used training-fold medians and evaluation covered out-of-fold discrimination, calibration, and reclassification.

claims.text: Trajectory features outperformed static summaries: AUROC 0.797 versus 0.755 and AUPRC 0.380 versus 0.304.
claims.poster_quote: Trajectory features outperformed static summaries: AUROC 0.797 versus 0.755 and AUPRC 0.380 versus 0.304.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Trajectory features reached 0.797 (0.794–0.800), a significant gain over baseline (∆AUC = 0.042; DeLong p < 0.001). Trajectory AUPRC was 0.380 versus 0.304 for baseline - a 25% relative improvement.
claims.reason: The results section explicitly states that trajectory features outperformed static summaries with AUROC 0.797 versus 0.755 and AUPRC 0.380 versus 0.304.

claims.text: Precision-recall performance achieved a 25% relative improvement at 11.1% prevalence.
claims.poster_quote: Precision-recall performance achieved a 25% relative improvement at 11.1% prevalence.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Trajectory AUPRC was 0.380 versus 0.304 for baseline - a 25% relative improvement and 3.4× the no-skill rate of 0.111.
claims.reason: The results section explicitly states that precision-recall performance achieved a 25% relative improvement at 11.1% prevalence.

claims.text: Signal persisted up to 12 months before diagnosis, enabling zero-burden preventive monitoring.
claims.poster_quote: Signal persisted up to 12 months before diagnosis, enabling zero-burden preventive monitoring.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Trajectory-based models maintained substantial discrimination across all horizons. AUROC declined gradually from 0.768 at the 3-month horizon to 0.740 at the 12-month horizon, demonstrating that biomarker trajectories contain predictive signal up to one year before diagnosis.
claims.reason: The results section explicitly states that signal persisted up to 12 months before diagnosis, enabling zero-burden preventive monitoring.

claims.poster_quote: Mean absolute SHAP importance on 5,000 held-out observations showed complementary contributions from biomarker levels and change.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: By mean |SHAP| on 5,000 held-out observations, the top physiologic trajectory features were BMI mean (0.141), systolic blood pressure mean (0.113), diastolic blood pressure slope (0.104), RDW mean (0.094), and systolic blood pressure slope (0.088).
